reason: The sources provide over a dozen cross-verified atomic facts across multiple independent sites detailing the cause, timeline, missed rescue, and aftermath of the Columbia disaster.
story: Eighty-two seconds into its twenty-eighth launch, Space Shuttle Columbia suffered an invisible blow: a piece of insulating foam broke off the external tank and struck its left wing. While the seven astronauts spent sixteen days in orbit conducting eighty scientific experiments, mission managers dismissed the impact as an accepted flight risk and cancelled requests for orbital imaging. On February 1, 2003, during atmospheric reentry, superheated atmospheric gases penetrated the breach, melting the aluminum wing structure. The orbiter entered an uncontrollable flat spin and disintegrated at over Mach 15 over Texas, killing all seven astronauts aboard. Remarkably, a biological canister of living roundworms survived the fiery plunge. After recovering eighty-four thousand pieces of wreckage, investigators concluded NASA could have theoretically mounted an emergency orbital rescue using shuttle Atlantis, but the crew was never even told of the lethal danger.
angle: A piece of foam breached Columbia's wing during launch, and while the crew worked in orbit completely unaware, a shuttle rescue was technically possible—but NASA dismissed the damage until it was too late.

claims.claim: Space Shuttle Columbia disintegrated during atmospheric reentry on February 1, 2003.
All seven crew members aboard Space Shuttle Columbia were killed during the disaster.
The fatal mission was designated STS-107 and was the 28th flight for orbiter Columbia.
Columbia was the first Space Shuttle orbiter to fly in space, debuting in April 1981.
During STS-107, the crew worked 24 hours a day in two alternating shifts to conduct approximately 80 science experiments.
The crew consisted of commander Rick Husband, pilot William McCool, Michael Anderson, David Brown, Kalpana Chawla, Laurel Clark, and Ilan Ramon.
Ilan Ramon flew on STS-107 as the first Israeli astronaut in space.
Approximately 82 seconds after liftoff, insulating foam broke off from the external tank bipod ramp and struck Columbia's left wing.
The foam strike punctured a hole in the thermal protection system of Columbia's left wing.
The wing breach allowed superheated atmospheric gases to enter the orbiter during reentry, melting its internal structure.
At 8:59:32 a.m. EST, Mission Control lost signal after commander Rick Husband's radio transmission began with 'Roger' and was cut off mid-sentence.
The crew likely survived the initial breakup of the orbiter but lost consciousness within seconds after cabin depressurization.
The Columbia Accident Investigation Board was chaired by retired U.S. Navy Admiral Harold W. Gehman Jr.
The accident investigation board concluded NASA could have evaluated launching Space Shuttle Atlantis on an emergency rescue mission to save the crew.
Search teams recovered approximately 84,000 pieces of debris across eastern Texas and Louisiana, representing roughly 40 percent of the orbiter's weight.
In the immediate aftermath of the disaster, individuals attempted to sell recovered Columbia debris on online auction sites including eBay.
A biological experiment containing live Caenorhabditis elegans roundworms survived the fiery breakup and impact with the ground.
The recovered non-crew debris was cataloged and stored on the 16th floor of the Vehicle Assembly Building at Kennedy Space Center.
Space Shuttle flights were grounded for more than two years following the disaster until Discovery launched on STS-114 in July 2005.
The Space Shuttle fleet was retired permanently in 2011 after completing assembly of the International Space Station.

disputed: Exact weight percentage of recovered debris: S1 states about 38 percent (84,900 lb), S6 states 84,147 lb, while S5 states nearly 40 percent; the script should say 'roughly 40 percent of Columbia by weight'.

Scheduled date for the final Hubble repair mission: S4 states it was scheduled for May 2008, while S1 and S5 note the mission ultimately flew as STS-125 in May 2009; the script should simply note it flew in 2009 after initial cancellation.
